clue.text: Rock overhead? It soared uncontrollably

indicators.note: something moving uncontrollably has no fixed course, so the preceding words fly apart into a new order

parts.note: the two words taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: Someone points at a rock in the sky that shot upward out of control.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'Rock overhead' is a playful definition: a rock in space rather than one on a cliff above you.
explanation.definitionFit: An asteroid is a rocky body orbiting the sun, literally a rock far above our heads.

clue.text: Overturned covers on boat to find small fish

indicators.note: in a down clue, something overturned is flipped upside down, so the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: tarps, short for tarpaulins, are waterproof covers stretched over boats

explanation.surface: A sailor lifts the boat's covers and discovers a little fish underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprat is a small silvery fish of the herring family.

clue.text: Herbal remedy expert resident in Eastern Oriental country

parts.note: standard abbreviation for Eastern

indicators.note: a resident lives inside a place, so one piece sits within the letters of another

parts.note: a country of the Orient
an ace is an expert

explanation.surface: A specialist in herbal medicine is living in an Asian country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oriental country' is the classic crossword cue for this nation; the expert sits inside it, after the compass letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Echinacea, from the coneflower plant, is a popular herbal supplement taken against colds.

clue.text: Physical science subjects showing evidence of time travel?

indicators.note: a traveller arrives somewhere new, so the lifted letter is set back inside the word at another spot
evidence of a journey means a letter is no longer where it started, so it is lifted out of its word

parts.note: topics are subjects of discussion
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: School science lessons apparently reveal signs that someone has been time travelling.
explanation.walkthrough: The T at the front of TOPICS travels two places along, turning TOPICS into OPTICS; the clue's time travel is literally a moving T.
explanation.definitionFit: Optics, the study of light and vision, is a branch of physics.

clue.text: Walked up, going over wet earth around new 6 (and 1)

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading the word from bottom to top

parts.note: trod is the past tense of tread, to walk

indicators.note: around means one piece surrounds another

parts.note: mud is wet earth
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A hiker trudged uphill, crossing boggy ground near something new.
explanation.walkthrough: 6 is CITY and 1 is ASTEROID: each such entry is a city that also names an asteroid.
explanation.definitionFit: Dortmund is a German city, and an asteroid has been named after it.

clue.text: Financial centre's maximum output after losing top area

indicators.note: losing something means it is taken away, so these pieces are dropped from the front of the word

parts.note: capacity is the most that can be produced
a cap is a top or lid
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A financial hub's peak productivity falls after it loses its leading district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'top area' looks like a single phrase but is two pieces lost from the front. The City is London's financial district.
explanation.definitionFit: The City of London is Britain's financial centre, so 'the City' is shorthand for high finance.

clue.text: Dotty about successful student of the vernacular

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word wraps around the other

parts.note: dotty means foolish or crazy
a successful student may earn an MA, a Master of Arts

explanation.surface: Someone is mad about a high-achieving student of everyday speech.
explanation.walkthrough: A successful student is one who has graduated, here with a Master of Arts degree.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatic language uses natural everyday expressions, the vernacular of native speakers.

clue.text: Climbing party accommodated in line, showing a calling for the mountains

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing means the letters read upwards, from bottom to top
something accommodated in a place is housed inside it

parts.note: a ley is a line, as in ley lines linking ancient sites
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A mountaineering group roped together in single file shows a vocation for the peaks.
explanation.walkthrough: LE(DO)Y is built first, then the whole thing climbs to read Y(OD)EL.
explanation.definitionFit: A yodel is a warbling call used by Alpine herders; the clue puns on calling as both shout and vocation.

clue.text: Successful periods getting good marks? Move on

parts.note: ups, as in ups and downs, are good times
a tick on work shows it is correct

explanation.surface: A run of good grades prompts someone to ask whether it is time to move on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up sticks' is a British idiom for packing up and leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: To up sticks is an idiom for leaving your home and relocating somewhere else.

clue.text: I'm moving into the French 6 (and 1)

indicators.note: moving into a home means going inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: la is French for 'the' (feminine)
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone announces they are relocating into a French house.
explanation.walkthrough: 6 is CITY and 1 is ASTEROID: the answer is a city that also names an asteroid.
explanation.definitionFit: Lima, Peru's capital, is a city that also has an asteroid named after it.

clue.text: 6 (and 1) favoured embracing right husband

indicators.note: embracing means holding something within your arms, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: a pet is a favourite, as in teacher's pet
R is the abbreviation for right
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A preferred place hugs a decent husband.
explanation.walkthrough: PE(R)T then H.
explanation.definitionFit: Perth, in Australia and Scotland, is a city that also names an asteroid.

clue.text: Bound to involve mistake if fearful

indicators.note: to involve is to take something in, so the following pieces are held inside

parts.note: tied means bound
to err is to make a mistake
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone frightened is sure to get something wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' looks like 'certain' in the surface; it is TIED: T(ERR IF)IED.
explanation.definitionFit: Terrified means extremely afraid, a strong synonym for fearful.

clue.text: Large bird with a sweet tail cut

indicators.note: with its tail cut, a word loses its final letter

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird
taken as written
sweet means nice, pleasant

explanation.surface: A big bird with a delightful tail that has been docked.
explanation.definitionFit: Titanic means gigantic, as befits the mythical Titans.

clue.text: Recalled strike's intent: raising a stink?

indicators.note: recalled is read as called back, so the words run backwards

parts.note: lams means strikes, as in to lam someone
an aim is an intent

explanation.surface: A recalled walkout's real purpose: to cause a fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strike's' stands for 'strike is', the verb in its third person: LAMS. LAMS AIM read backwards gives MIASMAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A miasma is a foul-smelling vapour, so miasmal things give off a stench; 'raising a stink' is literal.

clue.text: Not a 6 (but 1): trench remade with shortcut

indicators.note: something remade is rebuilt in a different form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: fodder taken as written
fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: A ditch is redug to take a quicker route.
explanation.walkthrough: 6 is CITY and 1 is ASTEROID: this is a small town, not a city, yet an asteroid bears its name.
explanation.definitionFit: Church Stretton is a small Shropshire market town in England, so not a city, though an asteroid is named after it.

clue.text: Not finishing university — new college appearing less stressful

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for university
N is the abbreviation for new
C is an abbreviation for college
something easing is becoming less tense

explanation.surface: A dropout leaves university; a new college looks less pressured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not finishing' looks like dropping a last letter, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Unceasing means never stopping, endlessly continuing without an end.

clue.text: Installs nastiest criminal

indicators.note: criminal suggests something crooked or bent out of shape, so the letters are twisted into a new order

parts.note: fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: A gang boss puts the most vicious crook in place.
explanation.definitionFit: To instate is to put someone formally into an office, which is to install them.

clue.text: Lie ailing with trauma — bacterial disease from California

indicators.note: ailing means unwell and out of sorts, so the letters fall out of their normal order

parts.note: fodder taken as written
fodder taken as written

explanation.surface: A patient lies sick and injured with an infection picked up on the West Coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Tularemia, or rabbit fever, is a bacterial infection first identified in Tulare County, California.

clue.text: See 15
Await game between rugby posts, supported by a figure from poetry

indicators.note: a game leg is a lame one, so the word is crippled into a different order
in a down clue, being supported by means sitting on top, so the next piece goes underneath
between puts something in the gap with one piece on each side

parts.note: each set of rugby goalposts is shaped like an H, and there is one at each end
fodder letters rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: Spectators wait for a match to start at the rugby ground, standing by a statue.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged AWAIT sits between two H shapes, with A beneath: H(IAWAT)H + A.
explanation.definitionFit: Hiawatha is the hero of Longfellow's narrative poem The Song of Hiawatha.

clue.text: Very noble, dismissing half through asking questions

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase for an adjective: Socratic means proceeding by questioning

parts.note: so means very

indicators.note: dismissing half sends away one half of the word, here its front

parts.note: aristocratic means noble

explanation.surface: An extremely aristocratic person sheds half their status by asking questions.
explanation.walkthrough: The first six of the twelve letters are dismissed, leaving the back half.
explanation.definitionFit: The Socratic method teaches by probing questions, as Socrates did in Plato's dialogues.

clue.text: Kitchen device more polished, cutting end of leek

indicators.note: cutting means removing, so a letter is taken out of the word

parts.note: slicker means smoother, more polished

indicators.note: 'end of' keeps only the last letter of 'leek'

parts.note: the last letter of leek

explanation.surface: A smarter kitchen gadget chops off the end of a leek.
explanation.definitionFit: A slicer is a kitchen appliance or tool for cutting food into thin pieces.

clue.text: Uncommon alarm about Conservative

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word wraps around the other

parts.note: a scare is an alarm or fright
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: Rare panic breaks out over the Tories.
explanation.walkthrough: SCAR(C)E. The Conservatives are Britain's right-of-centre party.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarce means in short supply, rarely found.

clue.text: 6 (and 1), as good when covered in warm light

indicators.note: something covered in another is wrapped by it, so it goes inside

parts.note: a glow is a warm light
taken as written
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A place looks as good as it gets bathed in warm light.
explanation.walkthrough: GL(AS G)OW.
explanation.definitionFit: Glasgow is Scotland's largest city, and an asteroid is named after it.

clue.text: Eighteen characters in pursuit of grand reptile

parts.note: G is short for grand, a thousand
the first eighteen letters of the alphabet run from A to R, written out as words

explanation.walkthrough: 'A to R' spans eighteen letters of the alphabet, so the phrase is spelt out literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A gator is a colloquial short form for alligator, a large reptile.

clue.text: Vocal piece with expression of surprise about length

explanation.walkthrough: G(L)EE.
explanation.definitionFit: A glee is a part-song for unaccompanied voices, popular in 18th-century England.

clue.text: Fruit in season, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is speech, so the word is judged by its sound rather than spelling

parts.note: something in season is current, available now

explanation.definitionFit: A currant is a small dried grape or a berry such as blackcurrant.

clue.text: Was bad? Was no good, missing first place

parts.note: failed means was no good

explanation.surface: A competitor who flopped asks whether they did badly, having missed out on first place.

clue.text: Cut economy initially — severe cut — a quarter

indicators.note: a cut word has been trimmed short, losing its last letter

parts.note: first letter of economy

explanation.surface: A budget report: trim spending, then make a harsh cut for a quarter.
explanation.walkthrough: A trimester is three months, a quarter of a year, though at college it is a third of the academic year.
explanation.definitionFit: A trimester is a period of three months, which is a quarter of a year.

clue.text: American rang up American, backing European 6 (and 1)
